dedupe_keys.name: emscher river conversion and green valley restoration against floods and heat ruhr germany

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes the conversion of the Emscher river in the Ruhr, Germany, which for a century carried the region's wastewater in open concrete channels with flows swinging from 11 to 350 cubic metres per second. The Emschergenossenschaft water association chose to move wastewater into closed underground sewers and to turn the river and its tributaries back into near-natural waterways with flood control areas, green spaces and habitat networks, aiming to reduce flood risk, cool the urban climate, store carbon and balance the water cycle in dry summers. The conversion began in 1992, the sewers took about 25 years and were due for completion in 2022, and ecological enhancement continues; with an investment of 4.5 billion euro over several decades it is one of Europe's largest infrastructure projects and was linked to about 1,400 jobs. The page is free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal, sourced from Emschergenossenschaft and Lippeverband. Caveats: climate benefits are described qualitatively and the page predates final completion. It illustrates large-scale combined wastewater and blue-green infrastructure planning for climate adaptation; a related record is the Physical Vulnerability Database for critical infrastructure.
name: Emscher river conversion and green valley restoration against floods and heat (Ruhr, Germany)
outcomes: Wastewater was moved underground and the Emscher system revitalised at a cost of about 4.5 billion euro from 1992 to 2022, creating flood retention, green corridors and cooler spaces.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study on the Emschergenossenschaft
resources_used: flood control areas and green spaces
